newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian opp'n hits Skase chase funds move.
newsitem.headline: Australian opp'n hits Skase chase funds move.

text.p: Australian opposition justice spokesman Nick Bolkus said on Thursday the government's decision to end funding for the recovery of assets from failed media tycoon Christopher Skase would open the country to fraud.
"We can't afford as a nation to basically put up a sign that says to all the white-collar criminals we're open for business again," Bolkus told reporters.
"If you're strong enough and you can outlast the government, if you can match the spineless attorney-general, then come back in and do the work as you used to in the '80s."
Media reports said Australian attorney-general Darryl Williams called off the chase because bankruptcy trustee Max Donnelly was unlikely to recover Skase's assets.
The asset search had already cost the government A$700,000, while A$14 million had been spent trying to extradite Skase from Spain, the Daily Telegraph newspaper reported.

However, Bolkus said Donnelly was making substantial progress in identifying assets and would shortly try to recover them. "I would have thought that once you've identified the assets, there's a sense of responsibility on the government to make at least initial steps to try and recover them," he said.
"Any interruption to the process now will jeopardise Donnelly's investigations and will make it even more difficult in the future to recover the assets."
Skase's entertainment and leisure group Qintex Ltd was put into receivership in 1989 with debts of about A$1.5 billion.
The failed tycoon declared himself bankrupt in 1991 with personal debts of A$80 million and then left Australia to live in Majorca, Spain.
According to media reports on Thursday, he took about A$10 million in cash and assets including jewellery, art and antiques with him.
Skase is still wanted in Australia to face company charges relating to his failed business dealings, but he remains safe while in Spain.
